title: Relational Model Rules
description: Understand Codd’s historical evaluation framework through concrete access, independence and integrity examples, while separating demonstrations from product certification.
notes:
## A historical framework for product claims

Codd's relational model rules are a historical framework for evaluating claims about relational database management systems. The familiar name is twelve rules, referring to rules one through twelve, with a foundation rule numbered zero. There are therefore thirteen numbered statements when the foundation is included. The framework addresses a whole system's capabilities rather than only how one table looks on a screen.

The practical question behind the framework is whether applications can manage facts relationally without depending on hidden record-navigation mechanisms. A product can offer table-shaped reports while still requiring lower-level operations for important work. Reading the rules as questions about observable capabilities is more useful than memorizing names alone or assuming that a product's use of SQL automatically establishes compliance with every criterion.

## Foundation and information representation

The foundation asks whether relational capabilities can manage the database fully. The information rule concerns explicit logical representation through table values. These are logical requirements, not instructions to store every physical byte in one particular disk format. A storage engine can use pages and indexes while presenting a relational logical interface to its users.

Consider a student ordering rule encoded only by the physical sequence of records. An application that assumes the first stored student is the class representative relies on information outside an explicit attribute. An attribute such as is_representative makes that fact visible in the logical model. It still needs appropriate validity rules, but readers no longer have to infer business meaning from a hidden storage arrangement.

## Address a value through its logical identity

Guaranteed access concerns locating a value through its relation, identifying key, and attribute. For example, Student, student_id seventeen, and programme identify a particular recorded programme without specifying a disk address. A query can express that lookup using a key predicate and an explicit selected column. Physical movement of the row should not redefine which student the identifier means.

```sql
SELECT programme
FROM students
WHERE student_id = 17;
```

This small query demonstrates a logical access pattern. It does not certify an entire product against the framework. An exercise can verify that a key lookup returns one intended fact, including a missing-key case, while a system evaluation requires broader evidence about all relevant data and interfaces. Keep the scope of a demonstration visible in the explanation.

## Missing information and discoverable descriptions

Systematic NULL treatment concerns handling missing information separately from ordinary zeros, blank strings, and other values. The catalog rule concerns representing database descriptions relationally so authorized users can query metadata using the relational language. Neither requirement says every user should obtain unrestricted access to all metadata or all student facts. Authorization still applies to the interfaces being evaluated.

A campus data tool may need to discover which columns a permitted table exposes before building a report. A queryable catalog can support that discovery without manually interpreting an opaque file layout. However, testing a fabricated metadata table only demonstrates query logic over that fixture. It does not prove that the actual database catalog exposes complete and correct structural descriptions under the required access rules.

## Language coverage and meaningful view changes

The comprehensive language rule covers more than SELECT syntax, including definition, manipulation, integrity, authorization, and transaction boundaries. The view-updating rule concerns views that are theoretically updatable. It should not be paraphrased as a demand that every arbitrary aggregate or combined result permit an unambiguous update. Some derived results do not specify a unique change to the underlying facts.

For example, a view exposing student identifiers and names has a different update interpretation from a report showing the average score of each programme. Changing one programme average does not say which individual scores should change or by how much. A lesson should explain that ambiguity before discussing product limitations. Actual view-update support requires testing the particular definition and operation on the intended engine.

## Operate on qualifying sets of facts

High-level insertion, updating, and deletion concern operating on relations or qualifying sets instead of requiring an application loop over individual records. One UPDATE can adjust every qualifying score using a clear predicate. The capability does not prohibit cursors or other additional interfaces; it requires the relational operation to be available for the appropriate task.

Suppose every recorded Computing score should receive five additional marks capped at one hundred. One statement can state that transformation. A row with an unrecorded score should remain unrecorded unless the business policy explicitly says otherwise. Correct set-based work still requires a precise qualifying population and expression. A single statement that updates the wrong students is not improved by being concise.

## Physical and logical independence differ

Physical independence concerns keeping logical application behaviour intact when storage representation or access methods change. An added index can change the chosen access path without changing which student facts a query requests. Performance may change; the logical answer and promised ordering should remain governed by the query contract rather than an assumed storage traversal.

Logical independence concerns appropriate information-preserving changes to the logical design while maintaining dependent behaviour where theoretically possible. For example, a compatible view might preserve an established result contract while underlying relations are reorganized. This is a demanding capability, not a promise that every arbitrary column removal or renamed public field can never affect callers. Real dependencies and supported transformations must be assessed explicitly.

## Integrity should survive alternative access paths

Integrity independence concerns defining constraints through the database language and catalog rather than relying solely on application code. Nonsubversion concerns preventing a lower-level interface from bypassing the integrity enforced through higher-level relational operations. These ideas complement one another: a declared rule is weak protection if an ordinary alternative write path can ignore it.

Imagine one registration form checks quantities but an import script writes invalid quantities directly. A database-enforced range rule can protect both paths where the engine supports it. This example illustrates the motivation, but a local CHECK test does not evaluate every import, administrator interface, or low-level engine capability. A product-wide claim needs a defined inventory of interfaces and direct evidence for the relevant allowed and rejected operations.

## Distribution concerns logical transparency

Distribution independence concerns preserving logical application behaviour when data distribution changes. Moving student facts among supported locations should not force applications to navigate physical sites as part of ordinary logical requests. This does not promise zero network cost, unlimited throughput, or perfect availability during failures. Those are distinct operational properties that need their own requirements and measurements.

A query fixture running on one local server cannot establish distribution independence. Likewise, one successful query after a storage change does not prove every independence property. Use these examples to formulate review questions, then identify which capabilities and transitions the chosen product actually supports. Avoid turning a conceptual framework into an unsupported benchmark result or a universal performance ranking.

## Use the framework with precise evidence

The rules are broader than domain, entity, and referential integrity alone, although integrity is an important concern within them. They are also different from a SQL syntax standard or a modern product feature checklist. A current compliance judgment must name the version, interpretation, supported configuration, interfaces, and evidence. Blanket claims that every product passes or no possible product passes are not justified by this lesson.

For study, connect each rule to an example and a limitation. Key-based access differs from physical navigation; set-based updates differ from mandatory loops; declared integrity differs from a form-only check. Then separate those demonstrations from catalog, view-update, distribution, and nonbypass verification that has not been performed. The framework is most useful when it improves the questions you ask and the accuracy of the claims you make.

questions.question_text: What are 'Relational Model Rules' most commonly a reference to?
options: Codd's twelve rules plus foundation rule 0, a historical relational-capability evaluation framework
The set of ANSI-approved data types
questions.explanation: The conventional twelve rules are numbered 1 through 12, with an additional foundation rule 0.

questions.question_text: What does Rule 1 (the Information Rule) require?
options: Database information is represented explicitly at the logical level through values in tables
Every query must run in under 1 second
Foreign keys are mandatory on every table
questions.explanation: The information rule describes logical representation; it does not prescribe a physical byte-storage format.

questions.question_text: Which rule requires that NULL values be handled consistently, distinct from all other values, regardless of data type?
options: Rule 3, Systematic Treatment of Null Values
questions.explanation: Rule 3 specifically mandates uniform, type-independent treatment of NULLs across the DBMS.

questions.question_text: How does Relational Integrity differ from Relational Model Rules (Codd's 12 Rules)?
options: They are the same list under different names
Relational Integrity is a narrow set of data-validity rules; Relational Model Rules is a much broader checklist evaluating an entire DBMS's relational completeness
Relational Model Rules apply only to NULL handling
Relational Integrity is broader and includes catalog and distribution rules
questions.explanation: Integrity (domain/entity/referential) is only a small part of the much larger 12-rule DBMS evaluation framework.

questions.question_text: Which rule requires that the database's own structural metadata (its catalog) be stored and queryable as relations, using the same query language?
questions.explanation: Rule 4 requires the catalog (schema metadata) to be represented relationally and queried the same way as ordinary data.

questions.question_text: What is needed before claiming a current SQL product satisfies every criterion in Codd’s historical framework?
options: SQL syntax support alone is sufficient
A version-specific evaluation of the relevant capabilities and interfaces with explicit evidence
Only a count of table names
A successful SELECT of one student
questions.explanation: This lesson does not establish a current product-wide compliance ranking. SQL support or one local example is insufficient evidence.

questions.question_text: Rule 7 requires support for high-level, set-at-a-time insert/update/delete operations. Does this mean row-at-a-time cursor processing is forbidden?
options: Yes, cursors violate Rule 7 and cannot exist in a relational DBMS
No — Rule 7 only requires that set-based operations be SUPPORTED; it does not forbid also offering row-at-a-time access
Rule 7 has nothing to do with insert/update/delete
Rule 7 only applies to SELECT statements
questions.explanation: Codd's Rule 7 mandates the availability of set-based operations; it doesn't prohibit additionally supporting row-at-a-time mechanisms like cursors.

questions.question_text: Which rule most directly overlaps with the concept of Relational Integrity (defining constraints independently of application code)?
questions.explanation: Rule 10 specifically requires that integrity constraints be definable in the data sublanguage/catalog rather than hard-coded into application programs.

questions.question_text: How many numbered statements are present when foundation rule 0 and rules 1 through 12 are included?
questions.explanation: The conventional twelve excludes the additional foundation rule.

questions.question_text: What distinguishes a logical student lookup from physical navigation?
options: It identifies a student by a declared key and requested attribute
questions.explanation: Key-based access avoids physical-position identity.

questions.question_text: Does the information rule prescribe one physical storage layout?
options: Yes; every value needs its own file
No; it concerns logical information representation
questions.explanation: Logical table values can have varied physical implementations.

questions.question_text: Does the view-updating rule imply every arbitrary aggregate result has an unambiguous update?
options: Yes; averages always identify one source change
questions.explanation: Some output changes do not determine unique underlying modifications.

questions.question_text: Which capability is illustrated by one UPDATE over all qualifying students?
questions.explanation: A predicate selects the affected facts without a required client row loop.

questions.question_text: Does support for set-based updates prohibit providing cursors too?
options: No; the required capability can coexist with additional interfaces
questions.explanation: The rule requires supported high-level operations, not exclusive interface choice.

questions.question_text: Which change most directly concerns physical independence?
options: Changing an access path while preserving logical query behaviour
questions.explanation: Storage and access methods differ from the logical contract.

questions.question_text: What does integrity independence emphasize?
options: Database-definable constraints rather than form-only rules
questions.explanation: The trusted data boundary should own supported integrity rules.

questions.question_text: An import path bypasses the rule enforced through ordinary relational writes. Which concern is most direct?
questions.explanation: Alternative lower-level access must not defeat relational integrity.

questions.question_text: Does a local single-server query prove distribution independence?
options: No; it does not exercise distribution changes
Only if it returns zero rows
questions.explanation: The required transition is outside the tested scope.

questions.question_text: What should a current product-wide compliance statement specify?
options: Version, interpretation, configuration and capability evidence
questions.explanation: A defensible evaluation has explicit boundaries.

questions.question_text: Why is an exercise’s scope statement important?
options: A small demonstration cannot certify every system rule
questions.explanation: Readers must distinguish illustrative evidence from comprehensive evaluation.

coding_problems.title: Demonstrate logical access by a student key
coding_problems.task: Return student_id and programme for student_id 17, using the identifying key rather than a name or result position. Return no rows if that identity is absent.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, student_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, programme VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, score INT NULL);
constraints: The primary key identifies a student; names can repeat.
edge_cases: The requested identity can be absent.
Matching names do not identify the requested student.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT student_id, programme FROM students WHERE student_id = 17;
coding_problems.explanation: This demonstrates a key-based access pattern. It does not certify product-wide guaranteed access or other historical rules.

coding_problems.title: Demonstrate a set-based score transformation
coding_problems.task: Using one UPDATE, add five to recorded scores of Computing students, capped at 100. Keep missing scores and all other programmes unchanged. Then return student_id and score for every student.
coding_problems.starter_sql: -- Write one set-based UPDATE, followed by the requested result query.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, student_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, programme VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, score INT NULL);
constraints: Supplied recorded scores are integers from 0 to 100.
These isolated updates modify scratch fixture rows only.
edge_cases: Scores close to the upper bound must be capped.
hints: Use a predicate for programme and recorded scores.
LEAST can cap the computed score.
coding_problems.solution_sql:
UPDATE students SET score = LEAST(score + 5, 100) WHERE programme = 'Computing' AND score IS NOT NULL;
SELECT student_id, score FROM students ORDER BY student_id;
coding_problems.explanation: One relational update handles the qualifying population. Correct results illustrate the set transformation without proving every historical DBMS criterion.

original_questions.question_text: Does any major commercial SQL DBMS fully satisfy all 12 of Codd's Rules to the letter?

Only NoSQL databases satisfy all 12 rules
Only Rule 0 is ever satisfied by any DBMS
original_questions.explanation: Codd's 12 Rules are widely regarded as an aspirational benchmark; in practice no commercial DBMS meets every rule completely.
